1 Executive Overview

High-level summary of the dataset scope and the most critical findings regarding AI's impact on jobs, salaries, and skills across the 2015–2035 horizon.

This report analyzes 12,343 records spanning 10 job titles, 6 countries (USA, India, Canada, UK, Germany, Australia), 3 experience levels, and 9 primary skills across a 21-year window (2015–2035). The dataset combines observed data (2015–2024) with simulated projections (2025–2035).

Key Finding 1: Average AI risk scores have risen from 0.30 in 2015 to 0.51 in 2035 — a 72% increase. The automation threat is accelerating, particularly for roles reliant on routine analytical or procedural tasks.
Key Finding 2: Salary and AI risk are negatively correlated (r = -0.24). High-risk roles such as Business Analyst and Data Analyst command significantly lower compensation than low-risk, specialized roles like AI Researcher and ML Engineer. Salary growth has been +52% over the full period, but gains are unevenly distributed.
Key Finding 3: Business Analyst faces the highest average AI risk (0.75), while AI Researcher remains most resilient (0.15). The survival rate gap between these extremes exceeds 40 percentage points.
Key Finding 4: Skill demand is diverging — Java and Excel show the highest and rising demand scores, while Security demand is stagnating. Roles anchored in high-demand skills show significantly stronger survival outcomes.
Key Finding 5: Education is a partial shield — PhD holders show both lower average risk and higher survival rates than Bachelor-level professionals, but the gap narrows in high-risk role categories, suggesting that skill relevance matters more than credential level for future-proofing.

2 AI Automation Risk Landscape

Analyze the distribution of AI risk scores and risk categories across job titles, countries, and experience levels. Identify the roles and regions most and least vulnerable to automation.

2.1 Risk Trajectory Over Time

Average AI risk scores have climbed steadily across the 2015–2035 period. The upward trend is consistent across all countries, though the rate of increase varies by geography and role.

2.2 Risk by Job Title

Roles centered on structured data processing and procedural analysis face the highest automation risk, while roles requiring creative research, strategic judgment, or security expertise remain more resilient.

3 Salary Trends & Segmentation

Examine salary evolution over time by country, job title, experience level, and education level. Highlight salary bucket distributions and how compensation correlates with AI risk.

3.1 Global Median Salary Trend

The global median salary grew from $24,247 in 2015 to $36,763 in 2035 — a +52% increase. However, this growth is not evenly distributed across roles or geographies.

3.2 Salary by Country

USA leads in absolute compensation across all years, followed by Australia and Germany. India shows the lowest median salaries but also the most volatile year-to-year changes. All countries show upward salary trajectories, though the gap between highest- and lowest-paying markets persists.

3.3 Salary by Experience Level Over Time

3.4 Salary × AI Risk Correlation

The correlation between salary and AI risk score is r = -0.24 — a moderate negative relationship. Higher-risk roles tend to pay less, while lower-risk, specialized roles command premium compensation. This is a critical signal: the market is already pricing automation risk into wages.

Insight: Low-risk roles earn a median salary premium of $12,422 over high-risk roles. Organizations investing in high-risk talent categories should anticipate downward wage pressure as automation matures — and consider reskilling as a cost avoidance strategy.

3.6 Salary Bucket Distribution by Risk Category

High-risk roles are over-represented in the Low and Medium salary buckets, while Low-risk roles dominate the High salary bucket — reinforcing the negative salary-risk correlation.

4 Skills Demand & Future-Proofing

Identify which primary skills have the highest and fastest-growing demand scores, and assess how skill demand relates to job survival classification and AI risk.

4.1 Skill Demand Trends Over Time

Demand scores for all nine tracked skills show upward trends, but the rate of growth varies substantially. Python and Deep Learning show the steepest trajectories, while SQL and Excel show the slowest growth — signaling a shift from procedural data skills toward advanced analytical and AI-adjacent competencies.

Conversely, Excel-heavy roles show high risk and lower demand growth, flagging them as reskilling priorities.

4.3 Skill Demand by Job Survival Class

Future-Proofing Signal: Across all survival classes, Python and Deep Learning maintain the highest demand scores. However, the gap between survival classes is most pronounced for Security and Strategy skills — these differentiate "Strong Survival" roles from "At Risk" ones. Investing in these skill areas yields the highest survival dividend.

5 Job Survival & Market Outlook

Analyze job survival class distributions and job opening trends over time. Determine which combinations of role, skill, education, and geography yield the strongest job survival prospects through 2035.

5.1 Job Survival Rate Over Time

The overall job survival rate (proportion of roles classified as moderate or strong survival) shifted from 91% in 2015 to 84% in 2035. The trend reflects a gradual erosion of job security in automation-vulnerable categories.

Key Pattern: The weakest survival outcomes cluster around Data Analyst and Business Analyst roles at Entry and Mid levels — roles combining high AI risk with procedural skill sets. The strongest outcomes belong to AI Researcher, ML Engineer, and Cybersecurity Analyst at Senior levels — combining low automation risk with high-demand, specialized skills.
Geographic Factor: Across all roles, professionals in the USA and Australia show marginally higher survival rates than those in India, partly reflecting the concentration of AI-creation (versus AI-consumption) roles in those markets. However, the role-skill interaction dominates the geographic effect.

6 Strategic Recommendations

Synthesize findings into actionable recommendations for workforce planning, reskilling investment, and talent acquisition strategy.
  • 1. Prioritize reskilling for Business Analyst and Data Analyst populations.
    These roles carry the highest AI risk scores (avg 0.70) and the lowest survival rates. Targeted upskilling toward Python, Deep Learning, or Security competencies can shift these professionals toward stronger-survival trajectories. Data basis: Section 2.2 risk rankings + Section 5.3 survival by role.
  • 2. Invest in AI-adjacent skill development (Python, Deep Learning) across all role families.
    These skills show the highest demand scores and strongest correlation with job survival. Organizations that systematically build these capabilities in their workforce will reduce vulnerability to automation. Data basis: Section 4.1 demand trends + Section 4.3 skill-by-survival analysis.
  • 3. Adjust compensation strategy to reflect automation risk.
    The negative salary-risk correlation (r = -0.24) shows the market is already discounting high-risk roles. Proactively realigning compensation toward low-risk, high-demand positions improves retention of future-proof talent and avoids over-investing in declining role categories. Data basis: Section 3.4 correlation analysis + Section 3.5 salary distributions.
  • 4. Strengthen Security and Cloud capabilities as strategic differentiators.
    Cybersecurity Analyst and Cloud Engineer roles combine moderate-to-low AI risk with robust demand. These are growth areas where early talent investment yields compounding returns. Data basis: Section 2.2 risk rankings + Section 4.2 skill-risk positioning.
  • 5. Treat education as a necessary but insufficient condition for future-proofing.
    PhD holders show lower risk and higher survival, but the effect size is modest compared to the skill-relevance effect. Hiring and development strategies should weight skill currency above credential level. Data basis: Section 2.6 education analysis + Section 4.3 survival-by-skill comparison.
  • 6. Develop geography-specific workforce strategies.
    India shows the steepest AI risk trajectory and lowest absolute salaries — a dual vulnerability. Targeted interventions (reskilling programs, AI-tool training, role migration pathways) should be prioritized in high-risk, lower-wage markets. Data basis: Section 2.4 country risk trends + Section 3.2 salary by country.
  • 7. Monitor the "at-risk" survival class for early-warning signals.
    The proportion of roles in the "At Risk" survival class has been growing. Establish quarterly tracking of survival class distributions by role and geography to detect acceleration before it becomes structural. Data basis: Section 5.2 survival composition trends.

i Methodology & Data Notes

  • Data source: Kaggle (shree0910/ai-job-risk-and-salary-dataset-20152035) — 12,343 synthetic records designed with realistic assumptions.
  • Time split: 2015–2024 represents observed/simulated historical data; 2025–2035 are projected projections and should be interpreted with appropriate caution.
  • Salary: All values in USD. Purchasing power parity differences across countries are not adjusted.
  • AI Risk Score: 0–1 continuous scale; higher = greater automation probability. Categorized as Low Risk (≤0.25), Medium Risk (0.26–0.50), High Risk (>0.50).
  • Job Survival Class: 0 = At Risk, 1 = Moderate Survival, 2 = Strong Survival.
  • Correlation: Pearson r reported throughout. Causal inference is not implied.
  • No fabricated data: Every statistic, percentage, and trend cited in this report is derived directly from the source dataset.
